section.title: Your Steadfast Love, O Lord
section.sectionRationale: A psalm of David contrasting the self-deceived heart of the wicked, who have no fear of God before their eyes, with the LORD's loving devotion reaching to the heavens, His righteousness like the mountains, and the fountain of life and light found in Him alone.
section.thesis: The self-deceived wickedness that has no fear of God before its eyes stands utterly overmatched by the LORD's loving devotion, which reaches to the heavens and holds the very fountain of life and light for all who take refuge in Him.
section.frameNote: Three movements: an oracle describing the wicked man's self-deceived heart, with no fear of God before his eyes (1-4); the LORD's expansive loving devotion, faithfulness, and righteousness, culminating in the fountain of life and light (5-9); and a closing prayer for continued loving devotion and protection from the proud (10-12).

units.label: No fear of God before his eyes

verses.text: An oracle is in my heart regarding the transgression of the wicked man: There is no fear of God before his eyes.
For his eyes are too full of conceit to detect or hate his own sin.
The words of his mouth are wicked and deceitful; he has ceased to be wise and well-doing.

Even on his bed he plots wickedness; he sets himself on a path that is not good; 
he fails to reject evil.

units.label: With You is the fountain of life

verses.text: Your loving devotion, O LORD, reaches to the heavens, Your faithfulness to the clouds.

Your righteousness is like the highest mountains; Your judgments are like the deepest sea. 
O LORD, You preserve man and beast.

How precious is Your loving devotion, O God, that the children of men take refuge 
in the shadow of Your {{kanaph|wings}}!
They feast on the abundance of Your house, and You give them drink from Your river of delights.
For with You is the {{mekor|fountain}} of life; in Your {{or|light}} we see light.
Extend Your loving devotion to those who know You, and Your righteousness to the upright in heart.
Let not the foot of the proud come against me, nor the hand of the wicked drive me away.
There the evildoers lie fallen, thrown down and unable to rise.

kanaph.gloss: Wing, edge, extremity. The image of taking refuge in the shadow of God's wings pictures the tender, protective care of a parent bird, echoed in Ruth 2:12 and taken up by Jesus longing to gather Jerusalem under His wings, Matthew 23:37.

mekor.gloss: Fountain, spring, source. David locates the very source of life itself in God, an image Jesus fulfills by offering living water that becomes in believers a spring welling up to eternal life, John 4:14.

or.gloss: Light. David declares that in God's light, humanity sees light itself, an image fulfilled in Jesus, the light of the world, in whom was life, and that life was the light of men, John 1:4, 8:12.

basic.context: David describes an inward oracle about the wicked man's heart, so full of conceit that it cannot even detect its own sin, plotting wickedness even while at rest. Against this bleak portrait, David sets the LORD's loving devotion, reaching to the heavens, His righteousness like the highest mountains and His judgments like the deepest sea, under whose wings the children of men find refuge, feasting on abundance and drinking from a river of delights, for with God is the very fountain of life and light. The psalm closes with a prayer that this loving devotion would continue toward those who know Him, protecting them from the proud and the wicked, who will themselves finally fall.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm should be read as a study in contrast, moving deliberately from the claustrophobic, self-deceived interior world of the wicked to the vast, cosmic expanse of God's loving devotion, teaching that no human wickedness, however self-assured, can compare to the scale of God's character.
basic.originalLanguages: David pictures the children of men taking refuge in the shadow of God's kanaph, wings, feasting at His house and drinking from His river, for with Him is the mekor, fountain, of life, and in His or, light, all humanity sees light itself.
basic.typology: The fountain of life and the light in which all light is seen, verse 9, anticipates Jesus, in whom was life, and that life was the light of men, John 1:4, who offers living water that becomes a spring welling up within believers to eternal life, John 4:14, and who declares Himself the light of the world, John 8:12.
basic.christ: Jesus is the fountain of life and the light of the world this psalm celebrates, fulfilling verse 9 completely: 'In him was life, and the life was the light of men,' John 1:4. He offers the living water David only pictures as a river of delights, promising that whoever drinks it will never thirst again, a spring welling up to eternal life, John 4:14. And the refuge David finds in the shadow of God's wings, verse 7, is echoed in Jesus's own lament over Jerusalem, longing to gather her children as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, Matthew 23:37.
basic.god: God is shown in cosmic, overwhelming terms, His loving devotion reaching to the heavens and His righteousness like the highest mountains, yet intimately near, sheltering the children of men under His own wings and satisfying them from the fountain of life itself.
basic.crossReferences: John 1:4 identifies Jesus as the life that is the light of men, fulfilling this psalm's picture of the fountain of life and light. John 4:14 shows Jesus offering living water that becomes an internal, eternal spring, fulfilling the river of delights this psalm describes. Romans 3:10-18 quotes language echoing verse 1 as part of Paul's case for universal human sinfulness, showing the desperate need every person has for the loving devotion this psalm celebrates.
basic.oneStory: David's contrast between the self-deceived heart of the wicked and the LORD's loving devotion, reaching to the heavens and holding the fountain of life and light, finds its complete fulfillment in Jesus Christ, in whom is life and light for the world, and who offers living water that satisfies forever all who take refuge in Him.

context.literary:
Psalm 36 is a diptych, two panels hung side by side so that the eye is made to compare them. The first, verses 1 to 4, is a portrait of one man's inner life. The second, verses 5 to 9, is a hymn to God's character, and it is built on a completely different scale. The first panel is small and closed: the wicked man's eyes, mouth, bed and path, all shut inside himself. The second panel goes up to the heavens and the clouds, out to the mountains, down to the deep, and back into a house with a table and a river. A short prayer, verses 10 to 12, joins the two, asking that the loving devotion of the second panel reach the person threatened by the first.

The divine name itself follows this design. The LORD, the covenant name, is missing from the body of the first panel: the wicked man has 'no fear of God', and that is the only place God is mentioned. The name first appears in verse 5, 'Your loving devotion, O LORD', as though the poem had to change worlds before it could say it. From then on it is nearly all address, 'You' and 'Your', where the first panel spoke of 'he' and 'his'.

The poem is also a study in two ways of seeing. The wicked man has 'no fear of God before his eyes', verse 1, and his eyes are 'too full of conceit', verse 2, so that he sees only himself. The psalmist answers, 'in Your light we see light', verse 9. Sight is either self-lit or lit by God. Movement matters too: the wicked man 'sets himself on a path', verse 4, and the psalm closes with the foot of the proud and the hand of the wicked kept from pushing the psalmist, and the evildoers 'fallen', verses 11 and 12.

The last verse is spoken almost as a scene, 'There the evildoers lie fallen', with the pointing word 'there', as though the psalmist can already see the place where they lie. The final picture is of people who are not able to rise, which stands in quiet contrast to those who 'drink' from the river in verse 8.
context.historical:
The superscription gives 'For the choirmaster. Of David the servant of the LORD', a title David also carries in the heading of Psalm 18. 'Servant' is a court word, and it marks the psalm as the reflection of a man who serves a king greater than himself, and who is therefore free to speak of what he has seen in the house of another master, the wicked man. No event is named. The psalm reads like the meditation of a king or a court poet who has watched the proud at work and set what he saw against what he knew of God.

David also speaks in the language of prophecy. The word 'oracle' in verse 1 is the technical term for an inspired utterance. It introduces Balaam's prophecies, Numbers 24:3, and David's own last words, 'the oracle of David son of Jesse', 2 Samuel 23:1. Peter says David 'was a prophet', Acts 2:30. To say 'an oracle is in my heart' is to claim that what follows was given to him, not merely figured out.

The second half is full of the sights of Israelite worship. The 'house' with 'abundance' is the sanctuary, where worshippers ate the meals of their fellowship offerings 'in the presence of the LORD your God' and rejoiced, Deuteronomy 12:7. In David's day the ark was in Jerusalem and the tabernacle at Gibeon, 1 Chronicles 16:39, and the psalm's 'wings' recall the cherubim whose wings 'overshadow the mercy seat', Exodus 25:20, as well as the eagle that spreads its wings over its young, Deuteronomy 32:11. The 'river' would have brought to mind Psalm 46:4, 'There is a river whose streams delight the city of God'.

The cosmic images, heavens, clouds, highest mountains and the deepest sea, are the furniture of the ancient world's picture of a three-storey universe. The psalm takes what any Israelite could see, the sky above and the mountains and the depths of the sea, and uses it as a measuring line for what cannot otherwise be measured.
context.canonical:
The psalm's lines about God's loving devotion belong to a family of verses that stretch it beyond measure. 'Your loving devotion reaches to the heavens, and Your faithfulness to the clouds', Psalm 36:5, is nearly identical to Psalm 57:10, and Psalm 108:4 says it 'extends beyond the heavens'. Psalm 103:11 says 'as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is His loving devotion for those who fear Him'. Each is a version of one conviction: God's covenant love has no ceiling.

The 'shadow of Your wings' is a recurring image of refuge, at Psalm 17:8, 57:1, 61:4, 63:7 and 91:4. Ruth's blessing that she had come to take refuge 'under whose wings', Ruth 2:12, shows how ordinary the picture was. The fountain of life turns up in Proverbs, where 'the fear of the LORD is a fountain of life', Proverbs 14:27, and in Jeremiah, where the LORD Himself is 'the fountain of living water' that His people have abandoned for broken cisterns, Jeremiah 2:13 and 17:13. Isaiah invites the thirsty, 'Come to the waters', Isaiah 55:1, and Zechariah looks to a day when 'living water will flow out from Jerusalem', Zechariah 14:8.

The opening portrait is used by Paul. He builds a chain of Old Testament quotations to show that all humanity is under sin, drawing on Psalm 14, Psalm 5:9, Psalm 140:3 and Isaiah 59, and he ends it with the last line of Psalm 36:1, 'There is no fear of God before their eyes', Romans 3:10-18. The psalm's description of the wicked man's heart becomes the last stroke of his indictment. In the Gospel of John, the psalm's pair of 'life' and 'light' is applied to Jesus, 'In Him was life, and that life was the light of men', John 1:4. The book of Revelation closes the canon with a river of the water of life and a city without need of the sun, Revelation 22:1-5.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David meant his hearers to understand something about sin's logic, and something about the scale of God, and to let the second reshape the first. He begins with a diagnosis. The wicked man's core problem is not a lack of intelligence but a lack of the fear of God, and this produces a strange blindness in which the man is too full of himself to notice or hate his own sin, verse 2. He talks deceit, he has 'ceased to be wise', and even in bed he uses the quiet hours to plan, verse 4. David wanted his hearers to see that this is a portrait, not of a monster, but of a way of life in which God has simply dropped out of view.

Then he turns the reader's eyes upward. The wicked man's world is very small, and the antidote is not an argument but a sight of God. Four attributes are laid out like a landscape, and the reader is invited to stand in it. The point is not merely informative. The psalm wants its hearers to take refuge, to feast, to drink, and to see, and the language turns the reader from spectator to guest.

The closing prayer shows what the psalm was for. David asks that God's loving devotion continue for those who know Him, and that the foot of the proud not push him aside. It is a prayer of a man who has looked at both worlds and knows which one he is asking to be kept in.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The first four verses describe. They are a portrait of a kind of person, and they should not be turned into a checklist for labelling neighbours. Paul's use of verse 1 makes the point: he applies it to everyone, 'There is no one righteous, not even one', Romans 3:10-18, including the person reading it. The right use of the portrait is self-examination. Anyone who plots on their bed, Micah 2:1, or finds themselves flattered by their own conceit, is meeting a description of their own heart.

Verses 5 to 9 are also description, not command, but they carry an implicit invitation: the children of men 'take refuge', 'feast' and 'drink'. The psalm does not tell us what to do in imperatives. It shows what God is like and lets the invitation come from the sight. The believer's part is to run to the shelter that is offered, and to keep coming for the feast.

The prayer of verses 10 to 12 is a pattern to pray. It asks for loving devotion and righteousness to continue, and for protection from the proud. It does not gloat: verse 12 speaks of the evildoers as fallen, in the perfect tense, as a matter of fact and not as a curse. We are not told to rejoice at anyone's ruin. We are shown a person who is anxious to stay where God is, and who trusts God about what becomes of those who refuse Him.

debates.question: Whose heart is the oracle in, 'my heart' or 'his heart', in verse 1?

views.label: 'In my heart': the psalmist's inspired insight
views.case: The Hebrew as it stands reads 'in the midst of my heart', and the BSB follows it: 'An oracle is in my heart regarding the transgression of the wicked man.' On this reading David, like a prophet, has received a word of insight about the true nature of wickedness, and the oracle is that the wicked have no fear of God.

views.label: 'In his heart': transgression speaks inside the wicked
views.case: Some ancient versions and many modern translations read 'his heart', so that Transgression itself delivers an oracle to the wicked man from within. The sinner listens to a counterfeit prophet, and the very language of inspiration is turned on its head. It makes the verse's contrast with true oracles sharper.

views.label: Either way, a mock oracle
views.case: Both readings agree that the word 'oracle' sets up a contrast. Whether in David's heart or the sinner's, it is a word about the wicked man's transgression, and the effect is to dramatise it as a message that is being heard and obeyed.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew text as it stands makes good sense and should not be changed without need. The alternative is worth knowing because it shows how ancient readers heard the verse, and it highlights the personification of sin as a voice. What matters for the psalm is that verse 1 ends on the same diagnosis whichever reading is taken: no fear of God before his eyes.

debates.question: Who are the 'children of men' who take refuge in verse 7, and how wide is the invitation?

views.label: All humanity
views.case: The phrase is a general one, 'sons of Adam', and it appears with 'man and beast' in verse 6 in a setting of universal care. On this view the psalm celebrates God's goodness to the whole human family, and the refuge is open to everyone.

views.label: The covenant people only
views.case: Verse 10 asks that God extend His loving devotion 'to those who know You' and His righteousness 'to the upright in heart', which suggests a narrower group. The feast and the river belong to those who dwell in God's house.

views.label: Offered to all, enjoyed by those who take refuge
views.case: The verb is what decides the matter: it is those who 'take refuge' who find the shadow of the wings. God's care reaches all, verse 6, and the invitation is open, while the benefits of verses 8 and 9 are for those who come. This fits the psalm's two panels.

debates.bearing: The third view respects both the breadth of the language and the specificity of verse 10. It also fits the New Testament, where the same God who 'preserves man and beast' invites everyone, and where the invitation must be answered, John 7:37 and Revelation 22:17.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm begins with the word ne'um, 'oracle', the prophet's formula for an utterance received from God, as when Balaam 'lifted up an oracle', Numbers 24:3, and when David begins his last words, 2 Samuel 23:1. It is followed by pesha, 'transgression', a word with the sense of rebellion against an authority, used of Israel's revolt against the house of David, 1 Kings 12:19, and of God's own charge that His children 'have rebelled against Me', Isaiah 1:2. So the poem opens with rebellion speaking in the language of prophecy, an inspired word turned upside down.

Verse 6 says the LORD's righteousness is 'like the highest mountains', literally 'mountains of God', and His judgments like the 'deepest sea', literally the 'great deep', tehom rabbah. The BSB reads the divine name in 'mountains of God' as a superlative, but it may also mean the mountains that are God's own. The 'great deep' is the same phrase used at the flood, when 'all the fountains of the great deep burst forth', Genesis 7:11, so the image holds two ideas together. The judgments are unfathomable, and they are also the kind of thing that once overturned the world. The next line, 'You preserve man and beast', uses the verb yasha, 'to save', of both people and animals, and recalls the ark, where 'God remembered Noah and all the animals and livestock', Genesis 8:1, and God's concern for the 'many cattle' of Nineveh, Jonah 4:11.

In verse 7 the word for 'precious' is yaqar, which also means costly or rare. It is used in 1 Samuel 3:1 of the word of the LORD that 'was rare' in Eli's day. To call God's loving devotion 'precious' is to say that it is both valuable and scarce in a world that does not have it. The psalm is surprised by grace.

In verse 8 the 'river of delights' is literally the 'river of Your Edens', from the plural of the word for delight, the same root as the name of the garden, where 'a river flowed out of Eden to water the garden', Genesis 2:10. Whether or not the poet meant it as a direct allusion, the language echoes the garden, and the psalm's abundant house is a place where the lost delights of Eden are given back.

The verb in verse 10, 'extend', is mashak, to draw out or prolong. It is the word God uses when He says, 'I have drawn you with loving devotion', Jeremiah 31:3. The psalmist asks that God's loving devotion be drawn out over time, that it continue and not run dry. The word 'know' in the same verse, in 'those who know You', is the ordinary Hebrew verb for personal, covenant knowledge, and it describes an acquaintance and not only an awareness.

typology.type: The shadow of God's wings, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The wings above the ark's mercy seat, Exodus 25:20, and the wings of the eagle that catches its young, Deuteronomy 32:11, stand behind the psalm's picture of refuge. Jesus takes the image as His own when He laments over Jerusalem, 'how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling', Matthew 23:37. The escalation is that the shelter is now a person who offers Himself in the flesh. The type falls short in that the psalm's refuge could be entered by all who ran, while the tragedy Jesus names is that it can be refused.

typology.type: The river of delights and the fountain of life, verses 8 and 9
typology.fulfillment: The river that flowed from Eden, Genesis 2:10, and the river that gladdens the city of God, Psalm 46:4, point to a source of life that people may drink from. Jesus says, 'whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst', John 4:14, and on the last day of the feast He cries, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink', John 7:37-38, and John explains that He spoke of the Spirit. The type falls short because the psalm's water is enjoyed in a sanctuary, while Christ's water lies within the believer, and the final river flows from 'the throne of God and of the Lamb', Revelation 22:1.

typology.type: The light in which we see light, verse 9
typology.fulfillment: The psalm claims that one sees only by God's light. Isaiah promised a day when 'the LORD will be your everlasting light', Isaiah 60:19-20, and Jesus says, 'I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness', John 8:12. Paul says that God 'made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ', 2 Corinthians 4:6. The correspondence is real, and it is fulfilled in a face, not just an idea. The type still awaits its end, when the city 'has no need of sun or moon' because 'the Lamb is its lamp', Revelation 21:23.

typology.type: The abundance of God's house, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: The meals eaten before the LORD at the sanctuary, Deuteronomy 12:7, and the table prepared in Psalm 23:5, are pictures of fellowship with God. Jesus says, 'I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger', John 6:35, and the story ends at 'the marriage supper of the Lamb', Revelation 19:9. Isaiah's invitation, 'Come, buy and eat without money', Isaiah 55:1, is now given in Christ's name. The type falls short in that the feast in the sanctuary was repeated and temporary, while the supper of the Lamb is the end of hunger.

study.christ:
The most striking link to Christ is the pairing of two words in verse 9, 'life' and 'light'. 'With You is the fountain of life; in Your light we see light.' The Gospel of John opens with the same pair, applied to the Word made flesh: 'In Him was life, and that life was the light of men', John 1:4. It is hard to read the two side by side without hearing an echo, and John's sequence fits the psalm's: the fountain of life becomes a person, and His life is what lets people see. Jesus then says both halves of the psalm in the first person, 'I am the light of the world', John 8:12, and 'the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life', John 4:14. He cries out at the feast, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink', John 7:37. What the psalm places with God, Jesus offers as His own to give.

The psalm leads to Christ also by the image of the wings. When Jesus laments over Jerusalem and says He longed to gather her children 'as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings', Matthew 23:37, He is taking on Himself the role of the God under whose wings the children of men take refuge. It is a claim of divine prerogative wrapped in the tenderness of a farmyard image. The psalm invites people to run to the shelter, and Jesus shows that the shelter has a voice and a face and is willing, though some are not. Malachi's promise of 'the sun of righteousness' rising 'with healing in its wings', Malachi 4:2, and in Zechariah's song the Dawn from on high will 'shine on those who live in darkness', Luke 1:78-79, make the same link between light and wings.

A third link is the cost. The psalm calls God's loving devotion 'precious', a word that also means costly. The New Testament tells how costly it was: 'God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us', Romans 5:8, and He is 'rich in mercy', Ephesians 2:4. The loving devotion that reaches to the heavens is shown to be measured at the cross.

A fourth link is in the contrast between the wicked man and Christ. The man has no fear of God before his eyes, and he is too full of conceit to see his sin. Isaiah says of the coming King that 'He will delight in the fear of the LORD', Isaiah 11:3. Jesus is the human being in whom the portrait of verses 1 to 4 is reversed. And He is also the answer to it: Paul quotes verse 1 as the last stroke in his case that all are under sin, and then the very next verses tell of the righteousness of God 'through faith in Jesus Christ', Romans 3:18-22.

A word of care. The psalm is not a coded prophecy, and its river and fountain are first the gifts of the sanctuary. The New Testament does not ignore that meaning. It says that what the sanctuary offered in shadow is found in the person of Jesus, and that is why His words to the thirsty and to the dark are so bold.
study.god:
Psalm 36 gives one of the Bible's widest views of God's character, and it does it by setting four attributes side by side: loving devotion, faithfulness, righteousness and judgments. The first two reach to heaven and cloud, the last two to mountain and deep. It is an unusual pairing, since it puts the tender words and the stern words in the same sentence. God's loving devotion and His judgments are not two moods but two dimensions of one character, and the poem measures both as vast.

The mountains and the deep are also different kinds of measure. Mountains are stable, and the LORD's righteousness is fixed and cannot be moved by pressure. The deep is hidden and unsearchable, and the LORD's judgments cannot be fully traced. Believers must therefore trust the justice that they cannot always see, while the wicked man, who lives at surface level, thinks that his iniquity will not be found out. The God of the psalm is not a comfortable God, but He is reliable.

The scope of His care is wide. 'You preserve man and beast', verse 6, and the 'children of men' shelter under His wings, verse 7. He does not save only the deserving, or only the chosen people, though the psalm goes on to speak of those who know Him. There is a generosity in God that runs beyond any single group, and Jesus later says that the Father 'causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good', Matthew 5:45.

He is also a source, and not only a supplier. Verse 9 does not say that God gives life. It says that with Him is the fountain of life. He does not hand out light as a separate thing. In His light we see. God is not merely the giver of good things; He is what makes them good, and the psalm suggests that to be cut off from Him is to be cut off from life itself. This is what the wicked man has done with his 'no fear of God', and it is why his world is small.

He is hospitable. A house with abundance, a river of delights, a table: God is host to a large and unlimited guest list. And the tension left open is between His universality and the psalm's final prayer, which asks for His loving devotion 'to those who know You'. God's care is wide, but knowing Him is the way to the feast.

For worship, the psalm teaches us where to look. When the world's noise is about the schemes of the proud, the answer is not to study them further but to lift the eyes to God's loving devotion, and to drink. It offers a way of praising God that is not clever but spacious, one that says 'How precious', and stops to be amazed.

crossReferences.note: Paul assembles quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah to show that all people are under sin, and finishes with 'There is no fear of God before their eyes', from Psalm 36:1. The psalm's portrait of one man's heart becomes the last word about the human condition.

Almost the same wording as verse 5: God's loving devotion 'reaches to the heavens' and His faithfulness 'to the clouds'. The two psalms give the same praise in different situations, one in a cave under threat and one in reflection on the wicked, and each shows how naturally the language of heaven-high love arises.

'As high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is His loving devotion for those who fear Him.' It gives the measure of verse 5 a precise direction: the height of heaven is the size of God's love, and it is aimed at those who fear Him, unlike the wicked man who has no fear.

Boaz blesses Ruth as one who has come to take refuge 'under whose wings' of the LORD. It shows the image of verse 7 in a human story, where a foreign widow finds shelter, and it fits the psalm's 'children of men' who take refuge in the shadow of God's wings.

The 'fountains of the great deep' burst open at the flood. Psalm 36:6 says God's judgments are like the 'deepest sea', literally the great deep. The link shows that the depth of God's judgments is not only mystery but also something that once overturned the world.

A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden. The psalm's 'river of delights' is literally a river of 'Edens', and the feast in God's house recalls the abundance of the garden. The psalm reads like a picture of Eden opened to those who take refuge.

God calls Himself 'the fountain of living water' and charges His people with abandoning Him to dig broken cisterns. It is the negative image of verse 9: the wicked man of the psalm is the one who has left the fountain and can only draw on himself.

'There is a river whose streams delight the city of God.' The river that gladdens Jerusalem and the river of delights in the house of God are neighbours, and they show how the sanctuary was a place where God's life was imagined as flowing out like water.

'In Him was life, and that life was the light of men.' The paired words of Psalm 36:9, life and light, appear here as a description of the Word made flesh. The connection is one of the clearest places where John sits in the psalm's tradition and finds its promise fulfilled.

On the last day of the feast Jesus invites anyone who is thirsty to come to Him and drink, and promises streams of living water. He speaks as the source that the psalm locates in God, and places the fountain of life in the person who is speaking.

Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem's children under His wings as a hen does, but they were unwilling. The psalm's shelter of the wings is here made personal and shown to be refusable, and Jesus claims for Himself the role of the God under whose wings people take refuge.

A river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, the tree of life is there, and 'the Lord God will shine on them'. It is Psalm 36:8 and 9 arrived at last: the river, the fountain, and the light in which the redeemed see.

study.oneStory:
The psalm begins with a heart in which God has dropped out, and that is where the biblical story turns. In the garden the man and woman listened to a voice that told them they could see for themselves, and they hid from God among the trees. The wicked man of verse 2 is what that decision looks like when it has run its course: eyes that see only self, a mouth that deceives, a bed used for planning harm, and no sense of his own sin. By Genesis 6:5 the thoughts of the heart are 'altogether evil all the time', and the psalm has caught the inner shape of that condition.

The rest of the psalm shows what the story sets against it. Its central claim is that with God is the fountain of life. Eden's river, Genesis 2:10, was the first picture of it, and the psalm's 'river of Your Edens' plays on the name. When the way to the garden was closed, the tabernacle and temple brought a small Eden back: cherubim on the veil and over the mercy seat, a house where God's people ate before Him, and the wings of Exodus 25:20. Psalm 36 sits in that world and is sung by people who took refuge there.

The story reaches its centre in Jesus. He is the fountain of life and the light who came into the world, John 1:4 and 8:12. He is the one who opens His wings to the children of Jerusalem, Matthew 23:37, and who at the last feast cries out to the thirsty, John 7:37. Paul uses the psalm's first verse to show the depth of the need, Romans 3:18, and the gospel that follows is the answer to it, since loving devotion that is 'precious', that is costly, reached down to sinners in the death of Christ, Romans 5:8.

The last chapters of the Bible give the psalm its full sense. 'To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life', Revelation 21:6. The river flows from the throne, there is a tree of life on either side, and 'the Lord God will shine on them', Revelation 22:1-5. The city has no need of sun or moon, because the Lamb is its lamp, Revelation 21:23. The wicked man's small dark world is replaced by a dwelling place of God 'with man', where He 'will dwell with them', Revelation 21:3, and where at last in His light we see light.

quiz.q: What does verse 1 say is missing from the wicked man's eyes?

options.text: The fear of God.
options.note: The psalm's opening oracle diagnoses the root of wickedness as the absence of the fear of God.

options.text: General moral awareness of right and wrong.
options.note: Close, since moral perception is involved, but the verse specifically names the fear of God, reverence toward Him, not moral awareness considered on its own.

options.text: Knowledge of the law's details.
options.note: The issue described is a lack of reverent fear of God, not merely ignorance of legal details.

options.text: Wealth and possessions.
options.note: The verse concerns the absence of the fear of God, not material lack.

quiz.q: According to verse 2, why can the wicked man not detect or hate his own sin?

options.text: His eyes are too full of conceit, or self-flattery.
options.note: The psalm diagnoses self-deception rooted in pride as the reason wickedness goes unrecognized by the wicked themselves.

options.text: He has never been taught right from wrong.
options.note: The text specifically attributes this blindness to conceit and self-flattery, not simply a lack of education.

options.text: He is simply careless and inattentive to his own actions.
options.note: Close, since inattention is part of the surface picture, but the psalm specifically roots this in conceit, active self-flattery, not mere carelessness.

options.text: God has hidden the truth from him.
options.note: The blindness described is self-inflicted through conceit, not something imposed externally by God.

quiz.q: What three qualities of God does David describe in verses 5-6 using expansive, cosmic imagery?

options.text: His loving devotion, faithfulness, and righteousness, reaching to the heavens, clouds, and mountains.
options.note: David deliberately uses the vastness of creation to picture the scale of God's character.

options.text: His power, wisdom, and knowledge, described in general terms.
options.note: Close, since these are true divine attributes elsewhere, but verses 5-6 specifically name loving devotion, faithfulness, and righteousness, not power, wisdom, and knowledge.

options.text: His wealth, power, and popularity.
options.note: The psalm's imagery concerns God's moral character, not material wealth or popularity.

options.text: His silence, distance, and hiddenness.
options.note: This contradicts the psalm's emphasis on God's expansive, actively displayed character.

quiz.q: What does verse 9 say is found with God?

options.text: The fountain of life, and light by which we see light.
options.note: This verse locates the very source of life and light in God Himself, fulfilled in Jesus, John 1:4.

options.text: The source of all wealth and comfort alone.
options.note: The verse specifically names life and light, a deeper and more foundational reality than material comfort.

options.text: General blessing, without specific mention of life or light.
options.note: Close, since blessing is implied, but verse 9 specifically and vividly names the fountain of life and light, not blessing in vague, general terms.

options.text: A hidden treasure available only to kings.
options.note: The verse describes life and light available to all who take refuge in God, not a treasure limited to royalty.

quiz.q: What does David pray for in verse 10, and what warning closes the psalm in verse 12?

options.text: That God's loving devotion would extend to those who know Him, closing with the image of evildoers fallen and unable to rise.
options.note: The psalm closes contrasting ongoing blessing for the faithful with the final downfall of the wicked.

options.text: That God would simply ignore the wicked rather than actively judging them.
options.note: Close, since the wicked's fate is in view, but verse 12 pictures active downfall, thrown down and unable to rise, not mere divine neglect or indifference.

options.text: That David would receive greater wealth than his enemies.
options.note: The prayer concerns loving devotion and righteousness, not material wealth comparison.

options.text: That the wicked would ultimately triumph.
options.note: This is the opposite of the psalm's closing image, evildoers thrown down and unable to rise.

questions: David diagnoses the wicked as too full of conceit to even detect their own sin. Where might self-flattery be blinding you to a sin you need to honestly confront?

David describes God's loving devotion, faithfulness, and righteousness using the vastness of the heavens, clouds, and mountains. What area of your life feels too small or too broken for God's character to actually reach?
David pictures people feasting at God's house and drinking from His river of delights. Where are you currently seeking satisfaction in lesser sources instead of the fountain of life God offers?
Verse 9 says in God's light we see light itself. How has following Jesus, the light of the world, changed the way you see everything else in your life?

The psalm closes praying that God's loving devotion would extend specifically to those who know Him. How would you describe your own relationship with God right now, someone who merely knows facts about Him, or someone who truly knows Him?

translationNotes.note: An oracle renders a Hebrew term elsewhere used for prophetic utterances, suggesting David's insight into the wicked man's heart carries the weight of divinely given discernment, not mere personal opinion.
The shadow of Your wings is a common Old Testament image of divine protection, echoed in Ruth 2:12 and taken up by Jesus in Matthew 23:37.
Fountain of life renders mekor, a term for a natural spring, source, or origin, here identifying God Himself as the very source from which all life flows.
